title: E-bike or scooter suddenly cut out: what to try, in order
summary: Most cutouts come from a low or loose battery, a brake lever that didn't spring back, a loose plug, heat, or water. Check the easy things first, in this order.
steps: Get fully off the road to a safe, visible spot before touching anything.
Turn your lights on if they still work, or switch on your phone flashlight.
Look at the display. Note any error code or battery level before restarting.
Squeeze and release both brake levers. Make sure each one springs all the way back.
Turn the system off. Remove the battery, check the contacts, reseat it until it locks.
Turn it back on with your feet off the pedals, then try the lowest assist level.
Check plugs you can see near the display, handlebar and motor. Push loose ones back in.
If the motor feels very hot, switch off and let it cool for several minutes.
Still nothing? Ride it like a regular bike in a low gear, or walk it.
If the same code keeps coming back, stop using assist and get the bike serviced.
warnings: Never open the battery case at the roadside.
If the battery is very hot, smokes, swells, leaks, hisses or smells strange, stop and use the battery cards. Call 911 if anything is burning.
prevent: Before each night ride, check the battery is charged and locked in, the brakes spring back, and the lights work.

title: Battery ran low: assist faded or quit on a hill
summary: When the battery gets low, some systems shut off motor help on purpose and save what's left for the lights. Climbing on a low battery can also cause cutouts.
steps: Check the battery gauge. A flashing or empty gauge usually means assist is used up.
Turn assist to the lowest level or off to stretch what charge remains.
Keep your lights on. Some systems keep a reserve just for lighting.
On climbs, drop to an easy gear and pedal gently, or walk the hill.
If assist comes back on flat ground, save it for where you really need it.
Plan a pickup or charging stop now, before the lights run out too.
warnings: Light reserve times differ by brand. Don't count on lights lasting all night.
Phones or gadgets charging from the bike drain the battery faster.
prevent: Charge to full before night rides and plan your turnaround point with charge to spare.

title: Power flickers or cuts on bumps: battery and plugs
summary: Power that cuts in and out on bumps often means the battery isn't locked in or a plug is loose. Reseating usually fixes it.
steps: Stop somewhere safe and switch the whole system off.
Remove the battery if it comes out. Look for dirt, sand or bent pins on the contacts.
Gently clean grit off with a dry cloth. Never use metal tools on the contacts.
Slide the battery back in until it clicks and locks. Tug it to confirm.
If the display comes off, reseat it firmly in its holder.
Look along the cables for any plug pulled apart. Push it straight back together.
Switch on and test. If it still cuts out on bumps, ride without assist and get service.
warnings: Do not use a battery with cracks, swelling, or crash damage until a dealer checks it.
Keep keys, coins and screws away from battery contacts. They can short it.
prevent: Wipe battery contacts clean and check the battery locks in firmly before riding on rough roads.

title: Motor won't help: brake cutoff switch stuck on
summary: Brake levers have switches that cut motor power when squeezed. If a lever doesn't fully return, the bike thinks you're braking and won't help.
steps: Squeeze each brake lever hard, then let go. Watch that it snaps fully back.
Push each lever forward by hand to make sure it's all the way home.
Look for a bent lever or grit jamming it. Clear it if you can.
Test each brake separately: does assist return after working one side?
Restart the system with your feet off the pedals, then try the lowest assist level.
If assist is still off, ride it as a normal bike or walk it home.
warnings: Make sure the brakes themselves still stop the bike before riding.
If the motor keeps pushing while you brake, stop riding that bike and get it serviced.
prevent: Keep brake levers clean and have a shop check a lever that feels sticky.

title: Overheated motor or battery: temperature cutout
summary: Systems protect themselves by cutting or reducing power when the motor or battery is outside its safe temperature range. Hot days and long climbs make this more likely.
steps: Pull over somewhere safe and switch the system off.
Move the bike into shade if you can. Keep the battery out of direct sun.
Wait several minutes for things to cool, then restart.
Ride on in a lower assist level and an easier gear to reduce load.
If it overheats again, stop using assist and ride or walk it home.
Never pour water on the battery or motor to cool it.
warnings: A battery that is very hot, smells, swells, or makes noise is a fire risk. Use the battery warning-signs card.
In cold, the same error can mean the battery is too cold. Warm it indoors before use.
prevent: On hot days use lower assist on long climbs and park the bike in shade.

title: Error code on the display: what to do
summary: Codes differ by brand, but most roadside fixes are the same: note the code, restart, reseat the battery, check plugs. If it returns, ride without assist and get service.
steps: Read the code out loud or snap a photo so you have it later.
Press any button to clear the screen, then switch the system fully off.
Wait a moment, then switch back on.
Still there? Switch off, remove and reinsert the battery, then restart.
Check nearby plugs and the wheel speed sensor magnet for anything knocked loose.
If the code comes back, ride without assist. You can always pedal it.
Once you're safe, look the code up in your bike's manual or on the maker's website.
warnings: Don't keep restarting a bike that smells hot or is smoking. Use the battery fire card.
After a repeating code, have the bike checked before your next ride.
prevent: Save a photo of your bike's error code list on your phone.

title: Cut out after rain, a puddle, or washing
summary: Normal rain and splashes are usually fine, but water in a plug or connector can cause cutouts. Dry it, don't force it.
steps: Switch the system off and move out of the water.
Remove the battery and wipe water off the contacts with a dry cloth.
Check plugs you can reach for water. Dry them and push them back firmly.
Let things air dry as long as you can before switching on.
If it still cuts out, ride without assist or walk it home.
Let the whole bike dry fully indoors before you charge it.
warnings: If the battery sat underwater, don't charge or use it. Have a dealer check it first.
Never submerge an e-bike battery or spray it with a hose or pressure washer.
Unplug any phone and close the USB port cover in rain.
prevent: Avoid deep puddles and never pressure-wash the bike; wipe it down with a damp cloth instead.

title: Pedaling a heavy e-bike with no power
summary: An e-bike can still be ridden like a normal bike with the power off. It's heavy, so gears and pacing matter more than strength.
steps: Shift to an easy, low gear before you start pedaling.
Spin the pedals lightly and quickly instead of pushing hard.
Shift down early, before hills, not halfway up.
Walk steep climbs. Pushing beats burning out.
Start braking earlier. A heavy bike takes longer to stop.
Rest in safe, lit spots and drink water if you have it.
Keep your rear red light or reflector visible the whole way.
warnings: Chest pain, fainting, or feeling like you can't go on: stop somewhere safe and call 911.
Throttle-only scooters can't be pedaled. Walk them instead.
prevent: Practice riding with assist off on a short, easy loop so you know your bike's easiest gear.

title: Using walk mode to push a heavy e-bike
summary: Many e-bikes have a walk mode that powers the bike at walking speed while you push it beside you. It needs some battery left.
steps: Stand beside the bike with both hands on the handlebar.
On many bikes walk mode won't start with assist set to off. Pick a low level.
Press your bike's walk button, then hold the button it asks for.
Walk alongside. It stops when you let go, brake, or go too fast.
Keep a firm grip. It can stop suddenly and roll back on hills.
No sidewalk? Walk near the left edge facing traffic, unless that side is unsafe.
If walk mode won't start, the battery may be too low. Just push.
warnings: Only use walk mode with both wheels on the ground.
California allows walk mode up to 3.7 mph on class 1 and 3 bikes. Buttons vary, so check your manual.
prevent: Try walk mode once at home in daylight so you know which buttons to press.

title: Will my battery get me home?
summary: Range drops with cold, headwind, hills, high assist, extra weight and low tire pressure. The display estimate assumes nothing changes, so plan with margin.
steps: Check the battery gauge and the miles you still need to cover.
Remember the range estimate assumes steady conditions. Wind and hills shrink it.
Rough check: if battery percent left is below the percent of trip left, act now.
Drop to the lowest assist level. That gives the most range.
Use easy gears and steady speeds; avoid hard starts.
Unplug your phone from the bike's USB port if it's charging.
If it's close, tell someone your route and plan a pickup point now.
warnings: Cold nights can cut range noticeably. Leave extra margin in winter.
Low tire pressure costs range and makes pedaling harder.
prevent: Check tire pressure weekly and note how much battery your usual commute really uses.

title: Cold night: battery weak or range dropping
summary: Lithium batteries give less power and range when cold. Keeping the battery warm before the ride helps more than anything on the road.
steps: Expect less range than on a warm day. Use lower assist from the start.
If you stop for a while, take the battery inside with you if it comes off.
Put it back in right before you ride, not long before.
If you get a temperature error, warm the battery indoors before restarting.
Don't charge a freezing battery. Let it reach room temperature first.
On ice or frost, start off without motor help so the tires don't spin.
warnings: Do not charge below 32°F (0°C).
Never heat a battery with a heater, flame, or hand warmer pressed against it.
prevent: Store and charge the battery indoors at room temperature and fit it just before you leave.

title: Battery died at night, far from home
summary: First get safe and visible, then decide: pedal, push, charge, or get picked up. Don't push a long way along a dark road if a pickup is possible.
steps: Move well off the road into a lit spot if you can, like a store lot.
Turn on any lights left. Keep the rear red light or reflector facing traffic.
Share your live location with someone and say where you're headed.
Decide: pedal it, use walk mode, or push. Check how far home really is.
If walking on a road with no sidewalk, keep to the left edge facing traffic.
Need a ride? Call someone you trust or a ride service that can carry the bike.
To charge, ask an open business for a wall outlet and stay with the charging battery.
Feel unsafe, hurt, or threatened? Call 911.
warnings: Never leave a battery charging unattended, even for a short trip inside.
Use only your bike's own charger, plugged straight into a wall outlet.
VVTA Micro-Link on-demand buses run weekdays 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. only. Not a late-night option.
prevent: Carry your charger, a small backup light, and a charged phone on every night ride.

title: Battery smoking, hissing, or on fire
summary: A lithium battery that smokes or burns is an emergency. Get away, keep others away, and call 911. Don't try to put it out.
steps: Stop and get off the bike right away.
Indoors: get out now, close the door behind you, and call 911 from outside.
Outdoors: step well back and keep other people away. Stay out of the smoke.
Call 911. Say it's a lithium e-bike battery fire and give your location.
Do not try to put out a battery fire yourself.
Stay back until firefighters arrive. Don't go back for the bike.
Never ride, charge, or reuse that battery again.
warnings: Smoke from battery fires is toxic. Keep upwind and well away.
Fire spreading to brush, a car, or a building: call 911 immediately and move away.
If you breathed smoke or got burned, tell the 911 operator.
prevent: Use only certified batteries and the original charger, and stop using any battery that swells, leaks, or smells.

title: Signs your battery is failing (or was damaged in a crash)
summary: Swelling, leaking, odd smells, strange noises, color change or too much heat mean stop using the battery now. Crash damage counts too.
steps: Stop using it now if it swells, leaks, smells, changes color, makes noise, or gets very hot.
Don't ride it and don't charge it. If it's charging, unplug only if safe.
If it is safe to do so, move it away from anything that can burn.
Call 911, then keep yourself and others well back from it.
Swelling, smoke, or hissing: don't touch it. Get away and call 911.
After a crash or hard drop, have a dealer inspect it before charging or riding.
Never open, repair, or rebuild a battery yourself.
Take dead or damaged batteries to a battery recycler or hazardous waste site, never the trash.
warnings: Smoke, flames, or fire spreading: get away and call 911. Use the battery fire card.
Replace with the maker's battery or an approved one, not a cheap unknown pack.
prevent: Look the battery over for cracks, swelling, or damage before every charge.

title: Charging an e-bike battery safely
summary: Many battery fires happen while charging, often at night. Use the right charger, a wall outlet, a safe spot, and be there while it charges.
steps: Use only the charger that came with the bike or a maker-approved one.
Look the battery over first. Don't charge if it's damaged or swollen.
Let a hot battery cool, and a freezing one warm, before charging.
Plug straight into a wall outlet. No extension cords or power strips.
Charge on a hard, dry surface. Never on a bed or couch, or in a bedroom.
Keep it away from doors, exits, and anything that burns.
Stay awake and nearby. Never charge while sleeping or away.
Unplug once it's full.
warnings: Only charge between 32°F and 104°F (0°C to 40°C).
Gets hot, smells, or swells while charging? Stop using it and see the warning-signs card.
Have a working smoke alarm where you charge.
prevent: Charge in the daytime while you're home and awake, outdoors or in a ventilated spot if possible.

If the battery comes off, bring it inside with you on hot days.
Don't charge it while it's hot. Let it cool to room temperature first.
Store it indoors, dry, and away from heaters and anything that burns.

Keep a smoke alarm where you store and charge it.

title: Is my e-bike or battery certified? (UL 2849, UL 2271)
summary: UL 2849 covers a whole e-bike electrical system, UL 2271 covers light-vehicle battery packs, and UL 2272 covers scooters and similar devices. Certified gear has a testing lab's mark on it.
steps: Look on the bike, battery, and charger for a testing lab mark and standard number.
E-bike system: look for UL 2849 or EN 15194. Scooters and boards: UL 2272.
Loose or replacement packs: look for UL 2271 or the maker's approval for your bike.
Since January 1, 2026, California bans selling e-bikes, batteries or chargers without accredited lab testing.
Used sales don't need the lab label, so check secondhand gear extra carefully.
You can search the product in UL's free Product iQ database.
Buy replacements from the brand or its authorized dealer, matched to your bike.
Skip rebuilt, reworked, or used-cell packs, even if they're cheap.
warnings: Certified batteries can still fail if damaged or misused. Charging rules still apply.
Check for recalls and report problems at SaferProducts.gov.
prevent: Before buying any battery or charger, confirm it's made or approved for your exact bike and carries a lab mark.

title: California e-bike classes 1, 2, 3: helmets, age, where to ride
summary: California e-bikes have fully working pedals and motors of 750 watts or less. Class 1 is pedal-assist to 20 mph, class 2 has a throttle to 20 mph, class 3 is pedal-assist to 28 mph.
steps: Find the class label on the bike. It lists class, top assisted speed, and wattage.
Class 1: assist only while pedaling, stops at 20 mph.
Class 2: throttle can move the bike alone, stops at 20 mph.
Class 3: pedal assist to 28 mph, needs a speedometer.
Class 3 riders must be 16 or older. Rider and passenger always wear helmets.
Classes 1 and 2: helmets required for riders and passengers under 18.
Trails and paths: local agencies and State Parks can ban e-bikes. Obey posted signs.
Bikes modified past 20 mph on motor alone, over 750 watts, or with pedals removed aren't e-bikes.
warnings: Local rules vary, such as sidewalk or park bans. Check your city's rules.
Pedal-less electric dirt bikes (e-motos) are not e-bikes and are banned on public roads.
Police can impound a class 3 e-bike ridden by someone under 16.
prevent: Know your bike's class before you ride paths, and wear a helmet every ride regardless of class.

title: California electric scooter rules
summary: Stand-up motorized scooters follow different rules than e-bikes: a driver's license or permit, 15 mph max, no passengers, and no sidewalk riding.
steps: You need a valid driver's license or instruction permit to ride one.
Riders under 18 must wear a fitted, buckled bike helmet.
Top legal speed is 15 mph, everywhere.
On roads posted over 25 mph, stay in a bike lane or separated bikeway unless local rules allow otherwise.
No passengers, and no riding on sidewalks except to enter or leave property.
Keep at least one hand on the handlebars at all times.
At night: white front light, red rear reflector, and side reflectors.
warnings: Cities may add their own scooter limits. Check local signs.
Throttle-only scooters can't be pedaled when the battery dies. Plan to walk.
prevent: Charge fully before night trips and keep a backup front light on you.

title: Riding or pushing at night: lights and reflectors
summary: California requires a front white light, rear red reflector, and pedal and side reflectors at night, and e-bikes need the rear red light or reflector at all times. When the bike's lights die, you need a backup.
steps: Lights out? Pull off the road before fixing anything.
Use a backup clip-on light. A light worn on you or your helmet also counts.
No light at all? Walk the bike and use your phone flashlight to see.
Make sure the rear red reflector or light is clean and facing traffic.
Wear something bright or reflective if you have it.
Ride where drivers can see you; slow down when you can't see ahead.
If you can't be seen safely, walk it on the left edge facing traffic.
warnings: On a dark road with no lights, walking is safer than riding.
Your phone is your lifeline. Save some battery for calls.
prevent: Carry a small charged backup light and keep reflectors on pedals and wheels.
